name: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
title: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
answer: Obligation and service level tracking covers the systems that watch what a contract actually requires once it is signed, including delivery dates, uptime commitments, response times, payment terms, notice periods and renewal windows. It sits inside contract lifecycle management, where the signed document stops being a drafting artefact and becomes a running set of duties owed by each party. The work spans extraction of the obligation from the text, a schedule or register that holds it, and monitoring against real events such as tickets, invoices and service metrics. It also covers the evidence trail that shows whether a commitment was met when a dispute or audit arrives.

sections.body: Obligation and service level tracking covers the systems that watch what a contract actually requires once it is signed, including delivery dates, uptime commitments, response times, payment terms, notice periods and renewal windows. It sits inside contract lifecycle management, where the signed document stops being a drafting artefact and becomes a running set of duties owed by each party. The work spans extraction of the obligation from the text, a schedule or register that holds it, and monitoring against real events such as tickets, invoices and service metrics. It also covers the evidence trail that shows whether a commitment was met when a dispute or audit arrives.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on a contract repository or CLM platform holding the executed documents, plus a structured obligation register that links each duty back to its clause and to the party that owes it. Service level tracking adds a feed from operational sources, typically ticketing systems, monitoring and uptime tools, billing records and calendars, so that measured performance can be compared with the contracted threshold. Extraction is usually done by a document model or a rules engine over the clause text, with the output reviewed by a person before it enters the register. Alerts, dashboards and escalation queues sit on top, and integrations push reminders into email, chat or the ticketing tool where the responsible team already works.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual sequence is to parse the executed contract, identify clauses that create a duty, and convert each into a record with an owner, a trigger, a threshold, a measurement source and a due date. Recurring duties such as monthly reporting or quarterly service credits are modelled as schedules, while one off duties such as a notice of renewal are modelled as dated events. Service levels are tracked by pulling the operational metric, comparing it with the committed level over the agreed measurement window, and recording the result with the underlying data attached. Exceptions are routed to the responsible team, and the register is kept current as amendments, waivers and renewals change the underlying obligations. Reviews are typically periodic, with the register reconciled against the contract set so that terminated or superseded documents stop generating alerts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are missed obligations, wrong thresholds extracted from ambiguous wording, and metrics measured over the wrong window or from the wrong source. Provenance matters here, so each tracked obligation should point to the clause it came from, the version of the contract, and the data used to judge performance, which is what makes the record usable in an audit or a dispute. Access control and retention rules apply because obligation registers often contain commercial terms, personal data and security commitments. Where automated extraction or scoring is used, a human review step and a documented correction path are common practice, and the site's wider material on AI regulation and case law is relevant background for teams building these controls. This is a description of practice and not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Tracking is moving from static registers toward continuous monitoring, where contract terms are connected directly to the operational systems that produce the evidence. Expect more work on standard ways to represent obligations and service levels so they can move between platforms, and more use of extraction models to keep registers current as contracts are amended. The harder problems are interpretive rather than technical, such as deciding what counts as a breach of a vaguely worded commitment and how much human judgement stays in the loop. As AI specific terms appear more often in contracts, tracking those duties will likely become a distinct specialism alongside the general obligation register.
